text: A low-interaction honeypot simulates a service minimally — just enough to look real from the outside without actually running the real thing underneath. A classic example emulates an open SSH port: it accepts a connection, presents a convincing banner, logs whatever username and password an attacker tries, and that's the entire interaction.

There's no real daemon and no real shell behind it. That thinness is the point: because nothing real is actually running, there's very little an attacker can exploit or pivot through even after figuring out it's fake. Low-interaction honeypots are low risk and low realism — cheap to deploy in bulk, safe to leave unattended, but they only capture the shallowest layer of an attack: a probe, a login attempt, a scan.

A high-interaction honeypot flips that tradeoff entirely. It's a real, fully-functional system — a genuine operating system and genuine services — that an attacker can actually log into and explore as if it were a real target. Because they're dealing with something real, attackers behave naturally: running real reconnaissance, trying to escalate privileges, attempting to install tools, maybe even trying to pivot further in.

That realism is exactly what makes high-interaction honeypots valuable for intelligence — defenders watch an attacker's actual playbook unfold. But it carries real operational risk: a system an attacker can genuinely use is a system they could abuse, potentially as a launching point elsewhere, if it isn't rigorously isolated. Without that isolation, it stops being a trap and becomes an actual foothold handed over for free.

In a real deployment, an attacker who gains access to an isolated, fully installed Linux honeypot can actually explore the filesystem, attempt privilege escalation to root, and try installing a backdoor — all of it observed and logged in detail, and all of it safely contained, because the box has no real route anywhere else on the network.

Most real deception strategies use both. Low-interaction honeypots get deployed widely and cheaply as broad tripwires catching early probing. High-interaction honeypots get deployed more selectively, carefully sandboxed, when the goal is deep intelligence on exactly how a specific attacker operates. Next up: deception technology beyond the single honeypot — honeytokens, decoy shares, and fake Active Directory objects.
